thm-fitting-subgroup-contains-its-centra.notes: I reconstructed Craven's Theorem 2.13 (Philip Hall) from the PDF itself — printed pp. 30-31, PDF pages 32-33 of finitegroups2012.pdf — rather than from memory, then transcribed it against the library's own lemmas. Four things checked rather than assumed. (a) THE NARROWING TO FINITE. Craven's Theorem 2.13 says 'Let G be a soluble group', while this item says finite solvable. That is not decoration: the proof needs F(G) nilpotent, which can fail for infinite soluble groups, and the library's def-fitting-subgroup-of-a-finite-group is a finite-group notion whose well-definedness rests on Craven's own Theorem 2.11 for finite G. provenance.statement is ai-altered for exactly this reason and the report says so. (b) THE DEDEKIND SUBSTITUTION IN STEP 7.1, which is the step most likely to be wrong because of the variable clash. lem-dedekind-modular-law-for-subgroups reads 'Let A,B,C <= G with A <= C. If AB is a subgroup of G, then A(B∩C)=AB∩C.' I instantiate its A:=F, B:=C, C:=A. Its hypothesis A<=C is F<=A, supplied by step 5.1 since A is the preimage of A/F. Its hypothesis 'AB is a subgroup' is 'FC is a subgroup', supplied by step 3.1 from the AB=BA clause of def-fitting-subgroup-of-a-finite-group, both factors being normal. Then FC∩A=A because A<=CF=FC, again step 5.1. Conclusion A=F(C∩A)=FD, as written. (c) STEP 9.1 DOES NOT USE THE UPPER/LOWER CENTRAL SERIES EQUIVALENCE, which is not on this page. The library defines nilpotence by the upper series, so the step computes there directly: Z_1(D)=Z(D) by def-upper-central-series, D/Z_1(D) abelian makes Z(D/Z_1(D)) the whole quotient, hence Z_2(D)=D. Craven phrases the same point as L_3(A∩C)=1 in the lower series; I deliberately did not transcribe that phrasing. (d) [D,D]<=Z(D) IN STEP 7.2 needs both halves and both are written: D<=A gives [D,D]<=[A,A]<=F by step 6.1, and D<=C=C_G(F) makes every element of D commute with every element of F and so with every element of [D,D], while [D,D]<=D closes it. COUNTEREXAMPLE SEARCH: the theorem is false without solvability — A_5 has F(G)=1 and C_G(1)=A_5 — and step 4.1 is exactly where solvability of G/F is consumed, so the hypothesis is load-bearing and placed. Within finite solvable groups I found no candidate; Q_8 is finite solvable with F(G)=Q_8 nonabelian, which refutes the REVERSE containment and is what the iff-reverse row records. The eight boundary rows were written from the proof text: G=1 empties the defining product; the upper series is used only at indices 0,1,2; the single selection anywhere is c in C outside F, which is the contradiction hypothesis itself rather than a choice. Disposition: sound as written.

lem-nontrivial-normal-subgroup-of-a-solv.notes: This is the claim Craven states inside the proof of Theorem 2.13, extracted as a named lemma because that proof runs long enough to want the decomposition. Checked: N is solvable by thm-subgroups-and-quotients-of-solvable-groups-are-solvable, whose Statement is 'Every subgroup and every quotient of a solvable group is solvable. No finiteness hypothesis is required' — so this lemma needs no finiteness and claims none, unlike the theorem that consumes it. n>=1 follows from N!=1 together with the definition's own 'the trivial group has derived length 0'. A=N^(n-1) is nontrivial by the leastness in that same definition, and abelian because [A,A]=N^(n)=1. Characteristic in N: each derived term is characteristic in the preceding one, and characteristicity is transitive. THE CASE THAT NEEDED WRITING DOWN is n=1: the iterated-characteristic chain of step 3.1 then has no links at all and the conclusion degenerates to N char N. An empty iteration is exactly the shape that reads as proved when it is not, so it is in the `degenerate` boundary row explicitly rather than left implicit. One citation worth flagging: step 2.2 gets 'A abelian' by applying thm-quotient-abelian-iff-contains-commutator-subgroup to the TRIVIAL normal subgroup of A. That is a licensed instance (1 normal in A, and A/1 abelian iff [A,A] contained in 1), not a widening of the cited theorem. COUNTEREXAMPLE SEARCH: the converse is false — A_5 x C_2 has a nontrivial abelian normal subgroup and is not solvable — so no biconditional is claimed and the iff-reverse row says that with the witness. Disposition: sound as written.

prop-complement-and-disjoint-union-axiom.notes: I did NOT transcribe Dembo's Remark, and that is the substance of this review. As printed after Definition 1.1.36 it offers 'A^c in L whenever A in L, instead of requiring that B\A in L whenever A subset B', keeping the increasing-limit clause. That axiom system is NOT equivalent to a lambda-system, and I have a witness I checked element by element: on X={1,2,3,4} the family D={emptyset,{1},{1,2},{3,4},{2,3,4},X} contains X; is closed under complements (emptyset<->X, {1}<->{2,3,4}, {1,2}<->{3,4}); is closed under increasing unions, since X is finite so every increasing chain in D terminates and its union is its last term; and yet {1,2}\{1}={2} is not in D, so the relative-difference axiom fails. The item therefore states and proves the form that IS equivalent — X, complements, COUNTABLE DISJOINT unions — which is also the form the coverage row's own heading names ('equivalent complement-and-disjoint-union formulation'). provenance is ai-altered on both components for that reason, and the discrepancy between the source's Remark and the harvested heading is recorded as a finding in research/frontier-15-alpha-step9.md. Both directions verified independently of the source. Forward: complements are relative differences from X; a pairwise disjoint family's partial unions are built by induction as complements of (X\B_n)\A_{n+1}; the partial unions increase, so the increasing-union axiom finishes it. Reverse: emptyset=X\X is in D, B\A is the complement of the disjoint union A ⊔ (X\B) which needs A subset B for disjointness, and an increasing sequence is disjointified by C_{n+1}=A_{n+1}\A_n. No choice principle: every set used is an explicit formula in the given families, so this is a ZF theorem, which the nonempty-choice row records. Disposition: sound as written.

ex-the-group-action-monad-and-its-algebr.notes: Transcribed from Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, section VI.2 'Group actions', printed p. 141, which I read from the PDF rather than from memory: 'TX = G x X, x -> <u,x>, <g_1,<g_2,x>> -> <g_1 g_2, x> ... define a monad <T,eta,mu> on Set. A T-algebra is then a set X together with a function h: G x X -> X ... these are just the usual conditions that <g,x> -> g.x defines an action of the group G on the set X.' The correspondence was checked against the library's own definitions rather than assumed. def-t-algebra-and-algebra-homomorphism gives the two laws a∘eta_A = 1_A and a∘T(a) = a∘mu_A; evaluated pointwise these read h(u,x)=x and h(g_1,h(g_2,x))=h(g_1 g_2,x). I checked the DIRECTION of the second, since h(g_1 g_2,x)=h(g_1,h(g_2,x)) is the (gh).x = g.(h.x) axiom of def-group-action and not its converse; the two clauses match exactly, neither weaker nor stronger. The homomorphism law f∘a = b∘T(f) evaluates to f(g.x)=g.f(x), which is def-equivariant-map-of-group-actions verbatim. ONE THING WORTH RECORDING: this monad is NOT the writer monad already on this page. ex-the-writer-monad-from-a-monoid is X x M with the multiplication acting on the right, whose algebras are RIGHT actions; I built G x (-) directly so that the algebras are LEFT actions in the library's sense, and cited no page-mate, so no B-page leaf edge is created either. Boundary: X = emptyset is a genuine algebra — T(emptyset)=emptyset and the empty map is the unique structure map — and every verification here is pointwise, so each holds vacuously; G=1 degenerates T to the identity monad. Both are in the rows. Disposition: sound as written.
